strengths: Addresses an important problem: efficient Gaussian rendering for wide-field-of-view and distorted cameras.
The PBF/CSF association scheme is practically interesting, and the reported runtime breakdown suggests efficiency close to optimized splatting while substantially exceeding BVH-based ray renderers.

Evaluation spans multiple pinhole and fisheye datasets and includes useful ablations on Gaussian scaling, association, transmittance, and BEAP supervision. The paper is generally well organized and explicitly acknowledges limitations involving ordering, self-attenuation, and overlapping Gaussians.
weaknesses: The central exact-integration derivation is mathematically incorrect. Equation B.5 treats the determinant |RS| as the scale factor of a one-dimensional ray segment, effectively asserting |RS Δu| = |RS||Δu|. Determinants scale volume, not line length; line-length scaling depends on both the covariance and ray direction.

Consequently, Equations 4/B.7 omit essential factors. For the Gaussian defined in B.1, the line integral contains sqrt(2π)/(ρ|Σ|^(1/2)sqrt(dᵀΣ⁻¹d)) in addition to exp(-D²/2). The factor sqrt(dᵀΣ⁻¹d)=||d_u|| is direction-dependent and cannot be absorbed into a fixed per-Gaussian opacity.

The proof in B.3 silently changes the transformed ray direction to a unit vector using only a rotation. A rotation can align the direction but cannot normalize its magnitude; reparameterizing the ray introduces precisely the missing 1/||d_u|| factor. Thus, the claimed first-principles density integral instead recovers the pre-existing maximum-response heuristic, undermining the main technical claim and title.

Several empirical claims are overstated. The paper says it achieves state of the art across all MipNeRF360 metrics, but EVER has higher SSIM in Table 4. It also claims superiority across all ZipNeRF metrics, although Table 3 shows worse LPIPS than EVER for pinhole-to-fisheye and substantially worse SSIM/LPIPS than FisheyeGS for pinhole-to-pinhole.

The broad claim of supporting arbitrary camera models is not established: experiments cover pinhole and central KB-style fisheye cameras, while the angular construction and mirror correction are not validated for non-central, omnidirectional, or other generic camera families.

Important comparisons discussed in related work, including 2DGS and HTGS, are absent from the quantitative evaluation. There are also no repeated-run statistics, and implementation details are insufficient to independently reproduce the reported quality/runtime tradeoffs without the promised future code release.

strengths: Addresses an important practical problem: efficient Gaussian rendering for wide-field-of-view and distorted cameras.
The proposed PBF association scheme appears computationally useful, with detailed stage-wise runtime, memory, and per-tile association measurements.
Evaluation covers several pinhole and fisheye datasets and includes component ablations, cross-camera tests, regional metrics, and qualitative comparisons.
The presentation is generally organized, and the appendices provide derivations, gradient formulas, implementation discussion, and per-scene results.
weaknesses: The central mathematical claim is incorrect. Equation B.5 equates the scaling of a one-dimensional line element under x=RSu with |det(RS)|, but line length scales as ||RS du||/||du||, which depends on direction; the determinant instead scales three-dimensional volume. Correspondingly, the exact integral of the normalized anisotropic Gaussian contains a factor proportional to 1/(|det(RS)| ||S^{-1}R^T d||), which is missing from Equations 4/B.7. This factor depends on both Gaussian shape and ray direction and therefore cannot generally be absorbed into a per-Gaussian opacity.

The proof in Section B.3 silently converts the transformed ray direction to a unit vector. A rotation can align the direction with the z-axis but cannot remove its norm; changing the ray parameter introduces precisely the omitted inverse-direction-norm factor. Thus the method computes a maximum-response kernel, not the claimed exact Gaussian line integral. This undermines the main exactness claim and the associated gradients.

The formulation integrates over an infinite line rather than the physical half-ray. The assertion that the negative-ray contribution is negligible is heuristic and is incompatible with the paper's repeated claims of a closed-form exact solution for arbitrary cameras.

The association is also not literally exact for Gaussian support: PBF bounds a finite lambda-sigma ellipsoid, typically with lambda=3, although a Gaussian has infinite support. Tiling further assigns every candidate Gaussian to every ray in a sub-frustum. These may be sensible approximations, but the paper does not quantify their error while repeatedly labeling the pipeline exact.

Several empirical claims overstate the tables. For example, on MipNeRF360 the method does not achieve the best SSIM, and in the ZipNeRF comparisons it does not win every SSIM/LPIPS column. Statements such as outperforming all methods across all metrics and setting a new state of the art across all metrics are therefore unsupported.

Experimental evidence cannot repair the invalid derivation and has additional limitations: no repeated-run uncertainty is reported, ScanNet++ and Aria use only selected subsets, runtime comparisons mix numbers obtained on different GPUs, and important reproduction details are deferred to an eventual code release or inherited configurations rather than specified fully. The claimed support for arbitrary cameras is also broader than the demonstrated central pinhole and fisheye models.

strengths: The paper targets an important practical problem: accurate, real-time Gaussian rendering for wide-field-of-view and generic cameras.

The PBF/CSF association scheme is an interesting engineering contribution, with strong reported reductions in per-tile Gaussian counts, memory consumption, and runtime compared with EWA- and UT-based association.

The empirical study is broad and generally well presented, covering pinhole, fisheye, egocentric, and cross-camera settings, with competitive baselines, regional evaluations, qualitative results, and useful component ablations.
The method reports compelling reconstruction quality and efficiency, including substantial gains in peripheral wide-FoV regions and rendering speed close to optimized splatting systems.
The limitations concerning depth sorting, self-attenuation, and popping artifacts are explicitly acknowledged.
weaknesses: The central mathematical claim is incorrect. Under the anisotropic transformation x=RSu+mu, a one-dimensional ray element does not transform by the determinant |RS|, as asserted in Eq. B.5; its scale depends on the ray direction. Consequently, integrating the stated normalized world-space Gaussian along a unit world-space ray produces an additional direction-dependent factor proportional to 1/(|Sigma|^{1/2} sqrt(d^T Sigma^{-1} d)). This factor is absent from Eqs. B.7/B.13 and cannot generally be absorbed into a single per-Gaussian opacity because it varies with viewing direction.

The proof of Theorem 1 silently replaces the transformed direction du=S^{-1}R^T d with a unit vector. Rotation can align du with the z-axis but cannot remove its magnitude without changing the integration parameter; the integral should contain a 1/||du|| factor. Thus, the proposed expression is essentially a maximum-response function rather than the claimed exact ray integral.

There is an additional inconsistency in Eq. B.12, where the manuscript defines D^2=(u_0^2+v_0^2)/2 despite using exp(-D^2/2); this conflicts with Eq. B.9 and introduces another factor-of-two error if interpreted literally.

Because the invalid integral is the basis for the differentiable renderer, gradients, ablations, and the headline claim of a 'closed-form projective-exact' formulation, the main technical contribution is not sound even though the resulting heuristic may perform well empirically.

The association is only exact for a chosen finite lambda-sigma ellipsoid, whereas a Gaussian has infinite support. The paper should precisely separate exact bounding of a truncated contour from exact Gaussian association and quantify errors versus lambda.

The evaluation lacks repeated-run variability or statistical testing, and some runtime comparisons use numbers from different GPU generations. Reproducibility is also limited by deferring the public code release until publication.
